reviews.title: Hi Bevel Team,
reviews.text:
Hi Bevel Team,

I have a feature idea that I think could make Bevel much more engaging and help users stay consistent.

I would love to see a Friends / Social feature where I can add my friends and optionally share selected health and lifestyle information with them, such as:

• Sleep and sleep consistency
• Recovery / Readiness
• Training and workout activity
• Daily steps and activity
• Nutrition and calorie/macronutrient adherence
• Hydration
• Overall daily routine consistency

It would also be great to have challenges between friends, for example:

• Best sleep consistency this week
• Most consistent training schedule
• 8,000–10,000 steps daily challenge
• Nutrition adherence challenge
• Recovery score challenge
• Weekly healthy routine streak
• Overall consistency leaderboard

The important part would be having full privacy controls, so users can choose exactly what information they want to share and who can see it.

I think this could make Bevel much more motivating because consistency becomes something you can build together with your friends rather than doing everything alone.

For example, I could have a small group of friends and see:
“Ahmed: 6/7 days training | 82% sleep consistency | 91% nutrition adherence”

Then we could compete in weekly challenges and motivate each other to maintain better habits.

I believe this would add a strong social accountability and gamification layer to Bevel while still keeping the focus on health, recovery, and performance.

I would personally use this feature and would love to see it in a future Bevel update.

Thank you!

reviews.title: AI is not Great
reviews.text:
really like Bevel’s underlying health and sleep data, but I’ve increasingly stopped using the AI guidance because I find it anxiety-provoking and sometimes inappropriate. I originally used the more technical/“nerdy” guide, but found it overwhelming, so I switched to the friendlier/supportive guide. Unfortunately, even that guide uses language that feels unnecessarily alarming and far more certain than the data supports.

For example, after a night in which I slept over 8 hours with excellent continuity, REM and deep sleep, the AI told me: “Your HRV tank is empty,” that my “nervous system is completely overtaxed,” and, most troublingly, “You aren’t recovering during sleep; you’re just unconscious.” That kind of language is frightening, especially in a health app, and presents speculative interpretation as though it were a medical conclusion.

I’ve had a similar problem with exercise guidance. When my recovery metrics have been low, the AI has essentially advised me not to exercise because I am supposedly too depleted or insufficiently recovered to tolerate it. I think there is an important difference between suggesting that someone reduce intensity or choose gentle movement on a low-recovery day and implying that they should avoid exercise altogether based primarily on wearable-derived recovery scores.

I would strongly encourage Bevel to make a clearer distinction between measured data and AI interpretation, reduce catastrophic or emotionally loaded language, and be much more cautious about behavioral recommendations involving sleep, recovery, and exercise. Phrases like “this may suggest increased physiological strain” would be far more appropriate than declaring that someone’s nervous system is “completely overtaxed” or that they are “just unconscious.”

I find the actual Bevel data useful. It is the AI interpretation that is making the app less useful to me, rather than more useful. A “supportive” guide should help users understand their data without making them frightened of their own body.

reviews.title: Seems better than WHOOP
reviews.text: I have been using bevel now for about a week only.  My initial impression is that it is significantly better than whoop.  It does a lot more.  This is probably why whoop is suing them.  BEVEL is using the data from my Apple Watch and presenting it in a useful manner.  In addition it has a useful food diary analysis program built in that actually works well.  It is not quite as good as MyNetDiary app but good enough.  In addition it has a good strength trainer built in which works with your watch .  It is much better than the whoop strength trainer.  This is not a rip off of whoop it is a complete health tracker that works with many of the health tracker devices that exist on the market. They have focused on the software and use everyone else’s hardware. It shows.  You can use it for free apparently but will not get the built in AI.  I have used the trial with the AI and find the AI very capable. I will pay the $99/year. It is a very fair price for the work these people have put in .

reviews.title: Wow!!
reviews.text:
If you want a health and recovery tracker that delivers deep insights without requiring proprietary hardware, Bevel is an absolute game-changer.
 Smart Recovery Metrics: It analyzes HRV, resting heart rate, sleep quality, and temperature to give you a clear daily recovery score, helping you balance rest and exertion.
 Seamless Apple Health Integration: It pulls data effortlessly from your Apple Watch, letting you get advanced metrics without buying extra gear.
 Advanced Strain Tracking: It goes beyond basic steps to track cardiovascular strain and muscular load, ensuring your workouts are truly balanced.
 Stunning Interface: The app is sleek, modern, and turns complex health data into clean, digestible charts and actionable daily advice.

reviews.title: Best I’ve Tried
reviews.text: I downloaded a few fitness tracking apps and this is the only one I kept. Overtime the assessment of my recovery and sleep seems spot on. It analyzes if I’m making progress with my cardio training, maintaining or overdoing it. I would give it at least a month or two of data before making decisions based on it. It is the first thing I check each morning after my sleep score.
